rubric:
# Binocular "reward" research brief

Goal: for each object in your batch file (lines `id|name|type`), estimate **how rewarding it is to look at through
binoculars** — the "wow"/satisfaction an amateur gets, NOT whether it's detectable. Ground every score in real
observer reports. The app already computes *visibility* tonight; reward is a separate, condition-independent measure.

## Reference setup
Typical astronomy binoculars (7x50 – 15x70, incl. 10x50 and 14x50 stabilized), object well placed (high), a
reasonably dark rural sky, no Moon. A scale point is about the experience, not the object's physical fame.

## Scale 0–10 (anchors — keep consistent across batches)
- 10: Pleiades (M45), Double Cluster (NGC 869/884), Andromeda Galaxy (M31) in a dark sky, Orion Nebula (M42), Hyades, Mel 20 (Alpha Persei).
- 8–9: M44 Beehive, M7, M8 Lagoon, Coathanger, Albireo (colour contrast), M13, Mizar–Alcor, M6, M24 star cloud.
- 6–7: M35, M36–38, M11 Wild Duck, M22, M4, M27 Dumbbell, M17, M41, M47, IC 4665, Kemble's Cascade, the Garnet Star (colour).
- 4–5: M81/M82 pair, M33 (big but very faint), M5, M15, M92, M3, M52, M103, M29, small but pretty clusters.
- 2–3: M57 (tiny, star-like at this power), M51 (faint smudge), small faint open clusters, M1 (faint patch).
- 0–1: faint Virgo galaxies (M91, M98, M99, M100 …), objects that are just a "faint smudge, barely seen" in binoculars.

Coloured/variable single stars are rated by their colour/variability interest (e.g. Garnet Star, R Leporis, Mira
near max). A plain bright white star with nothing special is ~1–2.

## Evidence to collect (web search; use several sources per object where possible)
Phil Harrington's "Touring the Universe through Binoculars" / Binocular Universe columns (Cloudy Nights), Gary
Seronik "Binocular Highlights" (Sky & Telescope), Steve Tonkin's BinocularSky, Astronomical League Binocular Messier
and Deep Sky lists, Cloudy Nights binocular forum threads, Stargazers Lounge, Sky at Night magazine, NASA/ESA/Hubble
object pages (for what's notable), Messier Marathon binocular reports, Webb Society, blogs. Note phrases like
"showpiece", "stunning", "breathtaking", "one of the finest", vs "faint smudge", "disappointing", "challenging".

## Output
Write JSON to `/tmp/claude-1000/-home-lorenzo/a76ea45a-6288-458e-8dbf-3d4be7e47d24/scratchpad/reward/out-<BATCH>.json`:
```json
[{"id":"M45","name":"Pleiades","reward":10,"confidence":"high|medium|low",
  "why":"one short plain sentence on what makes it rewarding (or not) in binoculars",
  "traits":["many bright stars","fits the field","blue-white colour","nebulosity in dark sky", ...],
  "evidence":[{"source":"Seronik, Binocular Highlights","url":"https://...","says":"short paraphrase/quote"}]}]
```
Use the `id` exactly as in the batch file. Include every object. Aim for ≥2 evidence entries per object; for very obscure
ones 1 is fine and set confidence low. Don't invent URLs — only cite pages you actually opened or saw in search results.
Traits vocabulary (use these where applicable, add others sparingly): many bright stars, rich star field, fits the field,
too big for the field, chain/pattern, recognisable shape, colour contrast, vivid colour, variable, double split,
bright core, nebulosity, dark lanes/structure, pair in one field, faint smudge, star-like, tiny, sparse, low contrast.
Return a one-paragraph summary when done (count, score histogram, notable surprises).
